gi4_conquest.topic: The 1967 conquests and the first Israeli decisions on them (June–November 1967)

claims.text: War of 5–10 June 1967: Israel took Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, the Golan Heights from Syria; UN-brokered ceasefire took effect 10 June; HISTORY.com: Israel 'had tripled in size'; some 20,000 Arabs and 800 Israelis died; Sinai returned to Egypt 1982.

Akevot: Israeli Military Intelligence estimated about 90,000 Syrian residents on the Golan (about 20,000 in Quneitra) three days after the occupation; the census of 10 August 1967 counted 3,936 Syrian residents in its final figures (6,396 in another count); most remaining were Druze in the northern villages.

Akevot: Israel's position was that residents left (Col. Shlomo Gazit: departure 'should not be seen as an expulsion'); the ICRC concluded 'most of the refugees were expelled either violently upon arrival of the armed forces, or under duress at a later stage'; Michael Comay in 1968 described 'the expulsion of Arabs from Quneitra, which has been going on for several months'.

Israeli government, 19 June 1967 (Israel State Archives, clause 561/563): in the morning, by 10 votes to 9, approved proposing peace treaties with Egypt and Syria 'that include security arrangements, based on the international borders'; the competing annexation-oriented version received nine votes; in the afternoon the formula for peace with Egypt [and Syria] on the basis of the international border was approved unanimously.

19 June 1967: the government did not agree on a proposal for Jordan and decided not to decide for the time being; the drafting committee agreed, except Moshe Kol, that the Gaza Strip should be annexed to Israel.

AIJAC (on the 2012 State Archives release): the cabinet was firm East Jerusalem would not be returned; the decision was passed to the US in secret; Egypt and Syria gave no positive answer; the Arab summit at Khartoum (September 1967) adopted 'no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it'.

gi4_movement.topic: The Movement for Greater Israel (Land of Israel Movement), its 1967 manifesto, signatories, trajectory, and the same-day dissent

claims.text: Posen Library: the manifesto's opening: 'The victory of the IDF in the Six-Day War placed the nation and the state in a new and fateful period'; 'Now the whole Land of Israel is in the hands of the Jewish people, and just as we have no right to give up the State of Israel, so too we are commanded to maintain what we have received from its hands: the Land of [Israel]'. Original Hebrew, 1967; full text restricted to registered users.
Einav (INSS 2017) quotes the same sentence from Aharon Ben-Ami, Sefer Eretz Yisrael HaShlema (the Movement, 1977), p. 10, and notes that 'commanded' (metzuvim) gives the text a religious tone.

+972 (Sheizaf, from Erel 2010): the Land of Israel ad ran in Yedioth Ahronoth on 22 September 1967 signed by 57 leading cultural figures incl. Nathan Alterman, Haim Gouri and S.Y. Agnon; it said 'no government in Israel is entitled to give up this wholeness'. The same day a 52-word Matzpen ad in Haaretz said 'Holding onto the occupied territories will make us a nation of murderers and victims' and 'Let's leave the occupied territories now'.

Einav: about half the founding declaration's signatories were writers or academics; named: Moshe Shamir, Yitzhak Tabenkin, Zerubavel Gilad (Labor movement); Alterman, Gouri, Hayim Hazaz, Agnon, Yaakov Orland, Rachel Yanait Ben-Zvi; Aharon Amir; Shmuel Tamir (Free Center); Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook. Founding essays, collected in HaKol: Gvulot HaShalom shel Eretz Yisrael (ed. Aharon Ben-Ami, 1967), appeared in Maariv, Haaretz, Davar and Lamerhav within about two months of the war.

Einav: the Movement's essays aimed at policy recommendations in a collective 'we'; Siach Lochamim (The Seventh Day), first published September 1967 (ed. Avraham Shapira), recorded kibbutz soldiers' doubts in a personal 'I'; Amos Oz's invitation: 'not a victory album, nor a collection of heroic deeds'. INSS abstract: the two currents mark the start of far-reaching changes in the Labor movement and religious Zionism and gradually split the Zionist camp.

Wikipedia: the Movement for Greater Israel was founded in July 1967, led by Avraham Yoffe; founders included Labor Zionists, Revisionists and writers (Alterman, Amir, Gouri, Yanait Ben-Zvi, Tabenkin, Yitzhak Zuckerman, Zivia Lubetkin, Eliezer Livneh, Moshe Shamir, Shmuel Katz, Zev Vilnay, Uri Zvi Greenberg, Agnon, Isser Harel, Israel Eldad, Dan Tolkovsky, Yoffe); aim: keep the captured territories and settle them.

Wikipedia: in the 1969 Knesset election the 'List for the Land of Israel' won 7,561 votes (0.6%), below the 1% threshold; before the 1973 election it joined Likud; Yoffe was its only MK (1973–76); in 1976 it merged into La'am, which stayed in Likud until merging into Herut in 1984; Moshe Shamir later sat for Likud and Zvi Shiloah for Tehiya.

Goldstein and Shilo (2022): the Movement for the Entire Land of Israel was founded by activist Labour movement members shortly after the June 1967 war; in the 1970s Gush Emunim effectively took the lead in the movement.

Kedem Auction 47 lot: dozens of the Movement's documents 1967–69, including a handwritten version of its principles platform, council member list, issues 2 and 3 of its biweekly Zot HaAretz, a petition against withdrawal from territories, protocols with Nathan Alterman's participation.

Lustick (1988): the Movement for the Whole Land of Israel was a secular, elite pressure organization founded two months after the Six Day War; its manifesto said 'The whole of Eretz Yisrael is now in the hands of the Jewish people'; after 1973 Gush Emunim eclipsed it and absorbed many participants; by 1977 it had virtually ceased to exist.
+972: Matzpen was founded in 1962 by four former Communist Party members; signatories of its September 1967 ad were unknown to the public and many had been Matzpen members.

gi4_allon.topic: The Allon Plan (1967–1976) and Gush Emunim (1974–1977)

claims.text: Allon Plan first version (27 July 1967) proposed Palestinian autonomy in two large West Bank enclaves; most ministers rejected it on 30 July 1967; the early-1968 revision dropped the Palestinian option for a Jordanian one with a corridor to Jordan through Jericho; Israel would keep the Jordan Valley up to the eastern slopes of the hill ridge, East Jerusalem, the Etzion bloc and (1968) part of the Hebron foothills.

Allon Plan: September 1968 offer to Hussein specified a 10–15 km strip along the Jordan and most of the Judean Desert; demilitarized West Bank; Hussein rejected it, insisting on Resolution 242; plan never officially endorsed by successive cabinets; designed 'to include as few Arabs as possible in the areas claimed for Israel' (ProCon, per Wikipedia); Golan: a Druze state idea; Sinai: most to return to Egypt; Gaza: first annexation, later within a Jordanian-Palestinian state; Kiryat Arba (approved 1970) marked its western edge near Hebron.
Pedatzur (Haaretz 2007, via Wikipedia) reports Allon saying in June 1967 'The last thing we must do is to return one inch of the West Bank' before he drafted the plan.

FRUS editorial note: the US followed secret Israel–Jordan contacts May–November 1968; 'In November the Israelis proposed an agreement based upon the "Allon plan," which posited Israeli control over the West Bank, while returning political control of some two-thirds of a demilitarized West Bank to Jordan'; Hussein grew skeptical and eventually broke off the talks.

Ford–Allon memcon, 11 October 1976: Allon referred to his Foreign Affairs article ('the terrain is important even in the modern age'), said 'we need some changes in the Green Line' and 'the debate is about giving less, not more'.

Gold (2000): Allon set out 'secure borders' in Foreign Affairs, October 1976: a strategic zone from the Jordan Valley to the eastern slopes of the ridge, about 700 of the West Bank's 2,100 square miles (about one-third); his thinking guided Labor and Likud plans; Netanyahu in 1997 called his ideas 'Allon-Plus'.

Lustick: Gush Emunim founded spring 1974 (name coined at Haim Druckman's home, February 1974) by rabbis, religious war veterans and NRP Young Guard activists influenced by Rav Zvi Yehuda Kook; key figures Hanan Porat, Moshe Levinger, Druckman; 'nonpartisan, extra-parliamentary'; sought 'permanent incorporation' of the whole Land of Israel and opposed Palestinian autonomy; first goal to mobilize against disengagement from Syrian territory, supporting a hunger strike against withdrawal from Kuneitra.

Lustick: eight attempts to settle near Nablus 1974–75, seven foiled by the army; Hanukkah 1975 about 2,000 supporters at Sebastia; after confrontation with the Rabin government and Defense Minister Peres, settlers allowed into the Kadum army camp; 20,000-person march May 1976; Sharon's September 1977 plan envisaged over one million Jews in the West Bank in twenty years; Likud spent about $400m 1977–81 and settlers rose from roughly 3,500 to 18,500; Gush attacked Begin in 1979 over Sinai and autonomy.
